prompt.context: Our client is the Dean of Kellogg School of Management. She has hired you to advise her on an idea, which struck her during the previous week – to consider starting a satellite campus of Kellogg in India.
prompt.question: Should Kellogg enter the Indian market by establishing a satellite campus? Please determine whether this makes sense and provide a recommendation.

clarifying_info.q: What is the strategic rationale for this move?
clarifying_info.a: India is a fast-growing economy with huge demand for MBAs. Kellogg's Dean believes that an India campus would help Kellogg become a Top 3 global MBA program. The caliber of India candidates is the same as in the US.

clarifying_info.q: What is the financial objective or timeline?
clarifying_info.a: The Dean wants the satellite campus to breakeven in 4 years.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the main competitors in India?
clarifying_info.a: Eight top-tier business schools: 7 IIMs (Indian Institutes of Management) and the ISB (Indian School of Business). The ISB already has a partnership with Kellogg for its pedagogy.

clarifying_info.q: How are students admitted to these schools?
clarifying_info.a: IIMs select based on CAT test results; ISB admits candidates based on the GMAT.
Indian MBAs cost $20k per year (US MBAs cost $70k). Indian schools don't offer scholarships but banks offer loans.
Kellogg would only launch the 2-year MBA program in India.

exhibits.title: Indian business schools
exhibits.shows: A table comparing IIMs and ISB on program description and cost. IIMs: 500,000 applications, top 6% CAT scores interviewed, 5 candidates interviewed per seat, 85% of admitted candidates matriculate. ISB: 70% of admitted students matriculate, two campuses with total class size of 1,400. Cost row shows INR 1,200,000 per year for IIMs; 1 USD = 60 INR. Note: total cost at Kellogg US is $70k per annum.

exhibits.title: Admitted students – expected admits per year
exhibits.shows: A table showing expected admits per year across Years 1-4. Year 1: 600 (7.5% of 8,000). Year 2: 600. Year 3: 900. Year 4: 900. Note: only source of revenue is the fee charged to students.

data.note: Only source of revenue is the fee charged to students

exhibits.title: Estimated cost structure
exhibits.shows: A table of fixed costs and annual variable costs over Years 0-4. Fixed costs: $100M (land) + $50M (support infrastructure) = $150M in Year 0. Annual variable costs: $30M in Years 1-3, $20M in Year 4.

framework: Market Attractiveness: Size the Indian MBA market (top-down or bottom-up), assess demand growth and customer willingness to pay
Competitive Landscape: Evaluate IIMs and ISB, understand admission processes, pricing, and differentiation opportunities
Revenue Potential: Determine number of students (market share), fee to charge, and total revenue trajectory over 4 years
Cost Structure: Identify fixed costs (land, infrastructure) and variable costs (salaries, marketing, SG&A, cost per student)
Financial Feasibility: Perform breakeven analysis against 4-year target, including cumulative profit/loss table
Risks & Qualitative Factors: Brand dilution, cannibalization of US campus, impact on rankings, job prospects for India graduates, government/regulatory considerations

questions.prompt: Part 1 – Structure: How would you approach this market entry problem?
questions.guidance: A strong answer splits the problem into qualitative and quantitative tracks. Qualitative: impact on Kellogg brand and rankings, faculty/pedagogy support, regulatory environment. Quantitative: market sizing (# of students), revenue (fee × students × years), costs (fixed + variable), breakeven analysis. The candidate should also flag cannibalization risk (Indian students currently attending Kellogg US).

questions.prompt: Part 2 – Market Sizing: Estimate the total addressable market of high-quality MBA applicants in India.
questions.guidance: Use a bottom-up approach from Exhibit A. IIMs: 500,000 applications × 6% interviewed = 30,000; 1 in 5 accepted = 6,000. ISB: 1,400 matriculated ÷ 70% = 2,000 eligible. TAM = 6,000 + 2,000 = 8,000 high-quality applicants. Then size in dollars: fee between $20k and $70k – $50k/year is acceptable; market size = 8,000 × $50,000 × 2 years = $800M.

math.setup: Bottom-up from Exhibit A. IIM pipeline: 500,000 apps → top 6% interviewed → 1 in 5 accepted. ISB: 1,400 matriculated / 70% matriculation rate = total admitted.
math.answer: Total addressable market: ~8,000 high-quality applicants; market dollar value ~$800M over a 2-year program

questions.prompt: Part 3 – Market Share & Breakeven: Assume 7.5% market share in Year 1. Using Exhibits B and C, build a 4-year revenue and cost table and determine whether Kellogg breaks even by Year 4.
questions.guidance: Students admitted each year pay for 2 years, so in Year 2 and beyond, prior cohorts' second-year fees add to revenue. Discount rate is zero (confirm if asked). Key insight: by Year 4 the cumulative deficit is only –$5M, meaning breakeven is achieved in early Year 5. The project is financially viable given rising revenue and declining variable costs.

math.setup: Admits: Y1=600, Y2=600, Y3=900, Y4=900. Fee: $50k/student/year. Variable cost: $30M/yr for Y1-Y3, $20M for Y4. Fixed cost (Year 0): $150M. Note: each cohort pays fee in year of enrollment AND the following year. No discount rate.
math.answer: By end of Year 4 the project is –$5M (does not technically breakeven in 4 years, but with Year 5 revenue trajectory breakeven is achieved in the first month of Year 5). The project is financially sound.

questions.prompt: Part 4 – Risk Analysis: What risks should Kellogg consider before launching this satellite campus?
questions.guidance: Candidate should generate risks across multiple dimensions. See brainstorming section for full list. Strong answers cover brand dilution, cannibalization, rankings impact, and job-market dynamics.

questions.prompt: Part 5 – Recommendation: Should Kellogg launch the satellite campus in India?
questions.guidance: Strong recommendation: Yes, proceed, but with caveats. Financially it is viable (breakeven in ~4 years). Strategically it supports the Top 3 global ranking ambition. However, brand dilution and cannibalization risks require careful mitigation before launch.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks and concerns should Kellogg evaluate before launching the India satellite campus?

categories.name: Brand Impact
ideas: No top US school has yet been successful launching in India – first-mover risk
Satellite campus might dilute the Kellogg brand if quality is perceived as lower
Need to ensure brand parity: Kellogg US MBA must equal Kellogg India MBA in employer perception

categories.name: Rankings Impact
ideas: India campus could improve rankings through diversity and international presence
Indian graduate salary data (adjusted for Indian PPP) may pull down reported average salaries, hurting rankings
Proximity to Asia could increase recruiter and applicant reach

categories.name: Cannibalization
ideas: 50–60 Indian students currently matriculate at Kellogg US each year
India campus may reduce the India applicant pool for the US program
Impact on US MBA candidate pool across all of Asia

categories.name: Job Prospects & ROI
ideas: Must demonstrate strong job placement and salary outcomes for India graduates
Premium for Kellogg India degree vs. IIM/ISB must justify the higher tuition ($50k vs. $20k/year)
Bank loan availability already exists; affordability is manageable

categories.name: Operational & Support
ideas: Parent campus pedagogical support needed to maintain quality at the satellite
Faculty recruitment and retention in India
Government land, infrastructure investment, and licensing approvals needed
$150M capital requirement may compete with Kellogg's new US building fundraising

categories.name: Financial
ideas: Breakeven not achieved until early Year 5 (4-year target missed by ~1 month)
50% jump in admitted class from Year 2 to Year 3 carries execution risk
Revenue growth assumptions rely on stable fee pricing at $50k

recommendation: Recommend proceeding with the India satellite campus. The project is financially viable, reaching near-breakeven by end of Year 4 and full breakeven in early Year 5, with a positive trajectory thereafter.
Strategically, the campus supports the Dean's objective of achieving Top 3 global ranking status by adding diversity, international presence, and access to Asia's talent pool.
risks: Brand dilution if the India campus is perceived as a lower-quality offering; requires rigorous quality control and marketing to maintain brand parity
Cannibalization of 50–60 existing Indian students in the US program, reducing diversity and net revenue at the home campus
Indian graduate salaries (at local PPP levels) may drag down reported average salary metrics, negatively affecting global rankings
$150M capital investment competes with other Kellogg fundraising priorities
Admission growth rate of 50% from Year 2 to Year 3 is aggressive and may be difficult to achieve
next_steps: Engage a brand agency to study the impact of a satellite campus on Kellogg's brand equity and employer perception
Secure funding for the $150M initial investment, potentially through dedicated India campus fundraising
Identify local and international partners for faculty support, marketing, and initial program delivery
Initiate discussions with the Government of India regarding land acquisition, subsidies, infrastructure investment, and regulatory licenses
Explore additional revenue streams such as executive education and corporate training to accelerate breakeven
